html:
The war by which Argentina took the Pampas and Patagonia from their Indigenous peoples, fought mainly from 1878 to 1885 under General Julio Argentino Roca. The "desert" was not empty: it was the land of the Mapuche, Ranqueles, Tehuelche and others.

For decades the frontier south of Buenos Aires had seen raids for cattle and Argentine punitive expeditions. In 1878 and 1879 Roca's columns, armed with breech-loading rifles and linked by telegraph, swept south to the Río Negro. Later campaigns pushed into the Andes and Patagonia until the last chiefs, such as Valentín Sayhueque, surrendered in 1885.

More than a thousand people were killed and more than fifteen thousand driven from their land. Prisoners were marched to Buenos Aires, held on the island of Martín García, and handed out as servants or sent to work on sugar estates. Families were broken up. Some smaller peoples did not survive as communities.

The land went to a small number of big owners for cattle and sheep. It helped make Argentina a great exporter of beef, wool and wheat and drew the mass migration from Europe that followed. Roca became president in 1880. Chile ran a similar campaign at the same time in Araucanía. In Argentina the campaign is now hotly argued over, and some of Roca's statues have been challenged. See also the Pampas peoples.
